title: The Key Discipline for Following Up
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece treats consistent follow-up as one of the most underrated leadership disciplines, arguing that even highly productive people often lack the planning needed to sustain momentum on initiatives. It lists the ordinary components of good follow-up, checking progress, providing support, keeping others informed, and argues the missing ingredient isn't effort but deliberate planning done before a meeting or task concludes. The article recommends identifying necessary follow-up steps at the close of any interaction rather than trusting memory or good intentions.
points: Weak follow-up, not lack of will, is identified as the common failure point for initiatives losing momentum.
The core follow-up actions (checking in, providing support, keeping others informed) aren't individually hard.
The fix is planning follow-up steps before concluding a meeting or task, not relying on memory.
Highly productive people's task lists are said to contain as many follow-up items as new responsibilities.
quotes: Without effective follow-up, the necessary momentum needed to work toward completion of an initiative often sputters and results in a disappointing outcome.
Everyone knows the essential ingredients of great follow-up: gathering more information, checking on progress, providing additional support, repeating a previous action.
The key to follow-up is to define what further actions are necessary to ensure progress before completing the last step.
Examine the task list of a highly productive leader or team member, and you will see as many follow-up actions as you do new responsibilities to be completed.
Great follow-up doesn’t just communicate excellence. It creates it.
